author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen expounds selected later passages of Matthew's Gospel, answering exegetical difficulties and correcting literalist misreadings, especially around the passion, the saying on eunuchs, and the Jerusalem controversies.
argument: Origen treats selected passages from Matthew, beginning with the title over the cross and the bribed soldiers' false report, then moving to the two great commandments and Christ's self-knowledge as Son of David according to the flesh and eternal Word according to the Spirit. He examines the Gethsemane and arrest scenes, emphasizing Christ's genuine human sorrow, Judas's inward betrayal, and Peter's rash promise and predicted denial, then turns to the woes against the scribes and Pharisees. He argues at length that the three kinds of eunuchs must be understood spiritually, not as a command to bodily mutilation, and that the rich young man's difficulty is not impossibility. Finally he interprets the request of the sons of Zebedee, the withered fig tree, the parable of the vineyard, the tribute to Caesar, and the Sadducees' question about the resurrection, consistently preferring the spiritual and moral sense over the merely literal.

outline.move: The passion narrative: the title 'King of the Jews' testifies to Christ's kingship, and the chief priests bribe the soldiers to spread a false report about the stolen body.

After the commandments of love of God and neighbor, Origen asks how all the law and prophets hang on these two commandments, and treats Christ's self-knowledge as Son of David according to the flesh and eternal Word according to the Spirit.
Gethsemane and the arrest: Christ's genuine human sorrow, his prayer concerning the cup, Judas's approach, the armed crowd, and Peter's rash promise and predicted denial.
The woes against the scribes and Pharisees: their simulated righteousness is dead, and they shut the kingdom of heaven while loading others with burdens.
The saying on eunuchs: Origen refutes two false interpretations and argues that all three kinds of eunuchs are spiritual, not bodily; then the children brought to Jesus and the rich young man.
The mother of the sons of Zebedee asks for seats at Christ's right and left; the withered fig tree teaches spiritual fruitfulness; the chief priests question Jesus' authority.
The parable of the vineyard, the comparison of parables where God is called a man, the tribute to Caesar, and the resurrection answer to the Sadducees.

cast.name: Jesus
cast.who: The central figure of the Gospel, interpreted by Origen as both Son of David according to the flesh and eternal Word of God.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The leading disciple, whose bold promise and threefold denial Origen examines.

cast.name: Judas
cast.who: The disciple who betrays Jesus, described as having already handed him over inwardly before the arrest.

cast.name: Scribes and Pharisees
cast.who: Jesus' opponents, accused of hypocrisy, false righteousness, and shutting the kingdom of heaven.

cast.name: Sons of Zebedee
cast.who: The two disciples called Boanerges by Jesus, whose mother asks for their seats in Christ's kingdom.

cast.name: Mother of the sons of Zebedee
cast.who: The unnamed woman who asks Jesus that her sons sit at his right and left.

cast.name: Sadducees
cast.who: Those who question Jesus about the resurrection and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.

cast.name: Herodians
cast.who: Mentioned as being with the Pharisees when they test Jesus about the tribute to Caesar.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: Mentioned only as the referent of 'the baptism of John,' which Jesus uses as a rhetorical question to expose the chief priests' hypocrisy.

cast.name: Micaiah
cast.who: The prophet in the books of Kingdoms who saw the Lord seated on a throne, cited among throne visions.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet who saw the Lord seated on a high throne, cited among throne visions.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: The prophet who saw thrones set and the Ancient of Days seated, cited among throne visions.

voices.speaker: Jesus
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly from the Gospel text, often introduced by 'he says' or embedded in the biblical citation.

voices.speaker: Origen
voices.how_marked: The commentator's own voice, using first-person singular and plural, introducing interpretations and refutations.

voices.speaker: Opponents or false interpreters
voices.how_marked: Introduced as 'some' (τινες) or 'others' (ἕτεροι) whose views Origen summarizes and refutes.

key_terms.sense: Those who are sexually inactive, understood spiritually as those who have cut off desire, not as the bodily mutilated.
The kingdom of heaven, the spiritual reign of God and Christ, contrasted with worldly kingdoms.
Those whose outward righteousness is a pretense, like whitewashed tombs full of dead bones.
The contrast between the literal text of Scripture and its spiritual meaning; the letter kills, the Spirit gives life.
The cup of suffering and death that Jesus asks to pass from him, yet accepts according to the Father's will.
To hand over or betray Jesus; Origen distinguishes approaching Jesus from approaching to betray him.
To stumble or fall away, as Peter was predicted to do before the cock crowed.
Counterfeit righteousness, dead because it is only outward show.
The seat of Moses, the teaching office claimed by the scribes and Pharisees.
The spiritual fruits listed by Paul, which the withered fig tree lacking them symbolizes.
The vineyard in the parable, representing Israel or the kingdom entrusted to new tenants.
The resurrection life in which there is no marriage, understood spiritually against the Sadducees.
The authority by which Jesus acts, questioned by the chief priests and revealed to those who bear fruit.

scripture: Origen cites the Gospels, especially Matthew, along with the Psalms, Isaiah, Daniel, and the books of Kingdoms. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint; modern citations should use the corresponding Hebrew numbering where they differ. Old Testament books are cited by their Greek titles (e.g., 'in Kingdoms', 'in the Psalm'); modern forms should use standard English names (1 Samuel, Psalms, Isaiah, Daniel).
uncertain: The precise date of composition of these later sections of the Commentary on Matthew.
The identity of the 'others' whose interpretation of the eunuch saying Origen refutes.
Whether the addressee or dedicatee of the commentary is named in the lost portions.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The passion narrative: the title 'King of the Jews' testifies to Christ's kingship, and the chief priests bribe the soldiers to spread a false report about the stolen body.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Congregati cum senioribus consilium acceperunt ut darent pecuniam militibus, ut dicerent: Discipuli eius nocte furati sunt eum, dormientibus nobis.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source mentions 'senioribus' (elders), not 'chief priests' specifically; it says they gathered with elders and took counsel to give money to soldiers. The bribery is attributed to those who had been reading 'Non falsum testimonium dices'—the Jewish leaders generally, not specifically identified as chief priests.

_unresolved_facts.claim: After the commandments of love of God and neighbor, Origen asks how all the law and prophets hang on these two commandments, and treats Christ's self-knowledge as Son of David according to the flesh and eternal Word according to the Spirit.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Post mandata dilectionis Dei et proximi quaeritur quomodo omnis lex et prophetae pendeant in duobus mandatis. Qui implevit dilectionem Dei et proximi dignus est sapientia et sermone scientiae per Spiritum, et exsultat in sapientia Dei.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 1 asks how all the law and prophets hang on the two commandments, and states that whoever fulfills love of God and neighbor is worthy of wisdom and word of knowledge through the Spirit. The 'self-knowledge' framing is not explicit; section 2 treats what the Savior knew about himself, not 'self-knowledge' as a category.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The saying on eunuchs: Origen refutes two false interpretations and argues that all three kinds of eunuchs are spiritual, not bodily; then the children brought to Jesus and the rich young man.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Δύο ἐσομένας περὶ τὸν τόπον τοῦτον παρεκδοχὰς πρὸ τῆς φαινομένης ἡμῖν ἀληθοῦς εἰς τὸν τόπον διηγήσεως ἐκθέμενοι... Τινὲς μὲν γάρ... Ἕτεροι δὲ οὐ πολλοὶ...
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen presents two prior interpretations (τινες and ἕτεροι) as two false approaches, then offers his own as the third/true one. The brief says he 'refutes two false interpretations,' but the structure is: two prior interpretations are presented, then both are found wanting, and a third (Origen's) is offered. The 'two false interpretations' framing slightly misrepresents the dialectical structure.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Sons of Zebedee — source_forms: ['duo filii Zebedaei', 'duo apostoli']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Προσελθοῦσα ἡ μήτηρ τῶν υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου (οὓς Βοανεργὲς ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Σωτήρ)... οἱ δύο ἀπόστολοι
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses 'οἱ δύο ἀπόστολοι' (the two apostles), not 'duo apostoli' (Latin). The brief mixes Greek and Latin forms without noting this. Also, 'duo filii Zebedaei' is not found in the source; the source has 'υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου' (Greek genitive plural).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Mother of the sons of Zebedee — source_forms: ['mater filiorum Zebedaei']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Προσελθοῦσα ἡ μήτηρ τῶν υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses Greek 'ἡ μήτηρ τῶν υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου', not Latin 'mater filiorum Zebedaei'. The brief should note the Greek form or use a consistent language for source forms.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἱ Φαρισαῖοι μετὰ τῶν Ἡρῳδιανῶν πειράζουσιν περὶ τοῦ κήνσου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses Greek 'Ἡρῳδιανῶν', not Latin 'Herodiani'. The brief should use the Greek form or note the language discrepancy.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ἀντερωτᾷ περὶ τοῦ βαπτίσματος Ἰωάννου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source refers to 'Ἰωάννου' (John), but in context this is 'the baptism of John'—the source form should be 'Ἰωάννου' (Greek genitive), not Latin 'Ioannes'. More importantly, the person is not explicitly identified as 'John the Baptist' in the source; he is simply 'John' in the phrase 'the baptism of John'.

The sections list is garbled and non-unique, mixing Latin and Greek sections without distinguishing them. The Greek sections (second set of 1-4, third set of 1-4, fourth set of 1-4, fifth set of 1-4) contain Jesus's words, but the Latin sections 1-2, 5-10, 3-4 also contain Gospel quotations. The brief should distinguish the Latin and Greek section sequences clearly.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τινὲς μὲν γάρ... Ἕτεροι δὲ οὐ πολλοὶ...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opponents/false interpreters appear in Greek sections 1-2 (the eunuch discussion), not in section 3. Section 3 presents Origen's own spiritual interpretation of all three eunuchs without opponent voices. The sections should be ['1', '2'] in the Greek sequence.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν Βασιλείαις εἶδεν Μιχαίας τὸν Κύριον καθήμενον ἐπὶ θρόνου
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'ἐν Βασιλείαις' (in Kingdoms), not 'the first of Kingdoms'. Micaiah's vision is in 1 Kings 22 (3 Kingdoms in LXX), not 1 Samuel. The mapping 'the first of Kingdoms' to '1 Samuel' is incorrect and not supported by the source.
This name does not appear anywhere in the provided source text. It should be removed from the names list.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint; modern citations should use the corresponding Hebrew numbering where they differ.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source cites 'in the Psalm' with 'Sit at my right hand' (Psalm 110 LXX / 109 Heb), but there is no explicit discussion of Psalm numbering in the source. The instruction about numbering is an editorial addition not grounded in the source text itself.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues at length that the three kinds of eunuchs must be understood spiritually, not as a command to bodily mutilation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οὐ χρὴ δὲ σωματικῶς ἀκρωτηριάζειν ἑαυτούς· καρπὸς γὰρ τοῦ πνεύματος καὶ ἡ ἐγκράτεια
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen explicitly states 'One must not mutilate oneself bodily' and that self-control is a fruit of the Spirit. However, he does not say the first two kinds of eunuchs are 'spiritual' in the same sense as the third; rather, he applies a tropological reading to all three: 'eunuchs tropically are those who are idle toward sexual matters.' The first two are 'by constitution' and 'by human reasoning,' while only the third is 'for the kingdom of heaven.' The brief flattens this distinction.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the rich young man's difficulty is not impossibility
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'he did not say impossible, but difficult' regarding the rich entering the kingdom. This is about rich people generally, not specifically 'the rich young man.' The brief personalizes what is a general saying in the source.
